title: The Transparency of Individual Compensation Is Fraught With Danger
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece pushes back against the trend of maximal organizational transparency by drawing a distinction between process transparency (how compensation decisions are made) and outcome transparency (individual pay figures). While the piece endorses openness about budgets, priorities, and criteria, it argues that revealing individual compensation specifically invites social comparison, resentment, and disputes that leaders can't fully resolve. It cites research suggesting high performers are often the most disgruntled once they see peer pay, and notes vague performance criteria make the resentment worse. The piece closes with a clear recommendation: keep the compensation process transparent, but never make individual pay figures visible.
points: Organizations tend to be more transparent about process than about outcomes.
Full transparency of individual compensation is identified as a step too far, unlike other categories of organizational openness.
Peer pay visibility increases social comparison, resentment, and disputes over fairness.
Research suggests high performers, not low performers, are often the most disgruntled once pay is visible.
The recommendation is to keep the compensation process transparent while keeping individual figures private.
quotes: Transparency in organizations creates buy-in and engagement.
In full-transparency workplaces, anything that directly affects team members is fair game and open to examination.
Transparency of individual compensation is fraught with danger for leaders and organizations.
Once team members are aware of peer compensation, comparisons intensify, feelings of undervaluation surface, and performance disagreements often become personal.
Research suggests it is high performers who are often the most disgruntled and feel the most underpaid.
The transparency of individual compensation is a train wreck waiting to happen.
